Joint Distributions and Dependence

How several random returns move together: joint and conditional laws, covariance, the multivariate normal, and what a normal model says about correlation in a crash.

Volume III · ProbabilityBuilds on LM1 · LM3 · LM5 · LM7 · LM8 · LM9 · LM10 · LM11 · LM12 · LM13 · LM14 · LM15Leads to LM17 · LM18 · LM19 · LM20 · LM21 · LM22 · LM23 · LM24 · LM25 · LM26 · LM27 · LM28 · LM30 · LM31 · LM32 · LM33 · LM35Time ≈ 3 h + labPDF A4 print edition
Learning Outcomes
MasteryAfter this module you should be able to:
1compute joint, marginal and conditional distributions from counts or a joint density, and decide whether random variables are independent
2define population covariance and correlation, prove ∣ρ∣≤1, and show that uncorrelated variables can be dependent
3compute the mean and variance of sums and portfolios, and explain why every covariance matrix is positive semidefinite
4apply conditional expectation, the tower property and the law of total variance
5describe the multivariate normal through linear maps, colouring, marginals and conditional distributions
6define the chi-square law, and interpret probability contours and the squared Mahalanobis distance against it
7compare a crash correlation with the bivariate normal benchmark under the same conditioning event
8compute joint frequencies, conditional moments, Mahalanobis distances and normal benchmarks in Python with the right divisor, guard and tail function
Learning Module Overview
  • A joint distribution holds the dependence that two marginal distributions miss. In U28, FinancialInsurance fell 1% or more on 40.4% of the days on which Semiconductor did, against 12.28% of all days.
  • Uncorrelated is not independent. The TAIEX price index's daily returns correlate 0.040 with the next day's, but their sizes correlate 0.183, and after a move of 2% or more the next day's size averaged 1.28% against 0.75%.
  • Covariance, correlation and covariance matrices are expectations. Under the empirical distribution they equal the sample statistics of Volumes I and II exactly, and every covariance matrix is positive semidefinite.
  • The variance of a sum adds covariances, (16.3). A model year of 245 uncorrelated days with the TAIEX price index's daily log-return moments has mean 13.36% and standard deviation 17.83%.
  • The tower property and the law of total variance split FinancialInsurance's daily variance of 1.482 (%²) into 1.140 within Semiconductor's three bins and 0.342 between them: 23.1%.
  • A multivariate normal vector is defined by its normal combinations. Colouring, whitening and the normal pair's conditional law follow, and the squared Mahalanobis distance has a chi-square law.
  • For the pair, a normal model with the sample's covariance matrix expects 48.68 days, with a standard deviation of 6.94, outside the whitened circle of radius 3; the data hold 177.
  • A normal pair with a constant correlation of 0.5749 gives 0.860 on days of 2-standard-deviation moves either way and 0.156 on joint falls of 2. The pair shows 0.788 and 0.669: only the one-sided events exceed the benchmark.

1Introduction

Volumes I and II measured co-movement in samples: LM7's covariance, LM8's correlation, LM10's covariance matrix and LM12's whitened returns. This module builds the probability model behind them, the joint distribution of several random returns. Under LM13's empirical distribution, each population formula gives back its sample formula exactly.

Motivating CaseDo correlations rise in a crash?

Semiconductor and FinancialInsurance are two of U28's sector indices. Over 4,382 daily returns, from 2 December 2008 to 8 October 2026, their correlation is 0.5749. Over 7–9 April 2025, the three sessions after the Qingming holiday, LM10 found 0.851. On 7 April both fell nearly 10%, the pair's most extreme day of the sample.

LM12 whitened the pair. In those coordinates 177 days lie outside the circle of radius 3. If the two returns were jointly normal with the sample's covariance matrix, about 49 would lie there.

So did the correlation rise in the crash, or would any sell-off look like this? What should a crash correlation be compared with, and how many extreme days does a normal model allow?

Exhibit 1 collects the case's numbers. Sections 2–5 build the tools, Section 6 the multivariate normal and the case's count, Section 7 the crash correlation, and Section 8 the Python.

NoteNotation for this module

Data: U28's T=4,382 daily price returns, A=245.48 (LM10). The pair is Semiconductor and FinancialInsurance; S5 adds Food, Plastics and ShippingTransportation. Moments divide by T (a bin's by its days). A model's correlation is ρ, a sample's ρ^​.

X, Y: random variables, set in each example; pX,Y​, fX,Y​, FX,Y​, pY∣X​, fY∣X​: joint and conditional pmf, density and distribution function; h(x):=E[Y∣X=x]; hi​: the functions of (16.1); S: a set of values of X, σS2​:=Var(X∣X∈S); X, R: random vectors, with mean μ, covariance matrix Σ (entries σij​, σii​=σi2​) and Corr(X):=diag(σi​)−1Σdiag(σi​)−1, while Σ^ and C stay the sample's; ai​, a: coefficients; M, b: a J×N matrix and a vector; L: the Cholesky factor, Σ=LL⊤, entries lij​ (no leverage here); β, ε: slope and residual of a normal pair; dt2​: day t's d2, LM12's ∥zt​∥2; n: the number of variables in (16.1) and (16.3), and a binomial's trials; p: the binomial's success probability. Counts: T (index t), N (indices i, j; also degrees of freedom), J, n, and m (days summed). A number of standard deviations is k≥0.

NoteResearch hygiene

Every count and correlation here describes U28's 4,382 days, 2 December 2008 to 8 October 2026 (sectors and the TAIEX price index): descriptive. The normal model and Example 5's model use the same days' moments: in-sample benchmarks, not forecasts. The lab's comparison of the two price-limit regimes is a stability check; whether gaps could be chance is LM21's and LM22's question. Example 2, Example 3, the knowledge checks of Sections 3 and 4, and Problems 2–4 and 9 are constructed.

2Joint, Marginal and Conditional Distributions

compute joint, marginal and conditional distributions from counts or a joint density, and decide whether random variables are independent

Start with counts. Pick one of the 4,382 days at random, each with probability 1/4,382: the empirical distribution of LM13. Let X be Semiconductor's bin that day: −1 for a return at or below −1%, 1 at or above 1%, 0 between. Let Y be FinancialInsurance's bin, defined the same way (Exhibit 2).

DefinitionJoint, marginal and conditional pmf

Let X and Y be discrete random variables on one sample space. Their joint pmf is pX,Y​(x,y):=Pr(X=x,Y=y). The marginal pmfs are its sums over the other variable, pX​(x)=∑y​pX,Y​(x,y) and pY​(y)=∑x​pX,Y​(x,y). For pX​(x)>0, the conditional pmf of Y given X=x is

pY∣X​(y∣x):=pX​(x)pX,Y​(x,y)​.

The marginal pmfs are the table's totals. The conditional pmf is (13.4) for the events {X=x} and {Y=y}: one row divided by its total. Read backwards, pX,Y​(x,y)=pX​(x)pY∣X​(y∣x) is the multiplication rule (13.5).

Example 1Reading the joint pmf

From Exhibit 2, find the probability that both sectors fall 1% or more, the two marginal probabilities and their product. Then find FinancialInsurance's probability of such a fall given a Semiconductor fall of 1% or more, and given a rise.

Solution

The joint probability is pX,Y​(−1,−1)=347/4,382=0.0792. The marginals are pX​(−1)=859/4,382=0.1960 and pY​(−1)=538/4,382=0.1228, with product 0.0241, which independence would make the joint probability (Section 3). The joint frequency is 3.29 times the product: a descriptive ratio, not evidence (LM21).

Given a Semiconductor fall, pY∣X​(−1∣−1)=347/859=0.404, against the marginal 0.1228. Given a rise, it is 20/1,004=0.0199. Knowing one bin changes the probabilities of the other.

For continuous returns, probability spreads over the plane with a density, as it spread along a line in LM5.

DefinitionJoint and conditional density

A joint density of X and Y is a function fX,Y​≥0 with

​Pr(x1​<X≤x2​, y1​<Y≤y2​)=∫x1​x2​​∫y1​y2​​fX,Y​(x,y)dydx​
for all x1​<x2​ and y1​<y2​. The marginal density is fX​(x)=∫fX,Y​(x,y)dy, and for fX​(x)>0 the conditional density is fY∣X​(y∣x):=fX,Y​(x,y)/fX​(x). The joint distribution function is FX,Y​(x,y):=Pr(X≤x,Y≤y).

By Fubini's theorem (LM5), a double integral equals an iterated integral in either order when the integrand is non-negative or absolutely integrable (stated without proof; Durrett 2019, Theorem 1.7.2). A marginal density integrates the other variable out.

Example 2A density on the unit square

Let fX,Y​(x,y)=x+y for 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1, and 0 elsewhere. Check that it is a density, and find fX​, Pr(X≤21​,Y≤21​) and fY∣X​. Are X and Y independent?

Solution

The function is non-negative, and

∫01​∫01​(x+y)dydx​=∫01​(x+21​)dx=1.​
The inner integral is the marginal, fX​(x)=x+21​ on [0,1]; by symmetry fY​(y)=y+21​. The corner square has probability ∫01/2​(2x​+81​)dx=161​+161​=81​.

The conditional density fY∣X​(y∣x)=(x+y)/(x+21​) changes with x: it is 2y at x=0 and 32​(1+y) at x=1. Knowing X changes the law of Y, so the two are dependent (Section 3).

PitfallThe marginals do not determine the joint law

The totals of Exhibit 2 also fit the table of independent bins, each cell the product of its marginals. That table puts 0.0241 in the corner where the data put 0.0792 (Example 1). Risk models with the same marginals can disagree completely about joint losses.

導讀聯合分布：一張表看兩個資產

只看每個資產自己的分布（distribution），看不出它們會不會一起跌。聯合分布（joint distribution）把「兩件事同時發生」的機率排成一張表，把列（row）或行（column）加總，就得到邊際分布（marginal distribution）。條件分布（conditional distribution）是把某一列除以該列的總和：半導體跌 1% 以上的 859 天裡，金融保險也跌 1% 以上的有 347 天，比例 0.404，遠高於不分情況時的 0.1228。連續型的情形把表格換成聯合機率密度函數（joint probability density function），把加總換成積分（integral）。同樣的邊際分布可以搭配完全不同的聯合分布，所以多資產的風險模型必須描述聯合分布本身。

Knowledge Check 1

From Exhibit 2, what is the probability that Semiconductor rose 1% or more, given that FinancialInsurance fell 1% or more?

Answer

Condition on the column: 20/538=0.0372, dividing by FinancialInsurance's falls, not by a row total.

3Independence, Covariance and Correlation

compute joint, marginal and conditional distributions from counts or a joint density, and decide whether random variables are independent
define population covariance and correlation, prove ∣ρ∣≤1, and show that uncorrelated variables can be dependent

LM13 called discrete random variables independent when their joint pmf is the product of their pmfs, (13.13). The general definition uses distribution functions, which every random variable has.

DefinitionIndependence and the product rule

Random variables X1​,…,Xn​ are independent when the first line below holds for all numbers x1​,…,xn​. Then the product rule, the second line, holds for all functions hi​ with E∣hi​(Xi​)∣<∞:

​Pr(X1​≤x1​,…,Xn​≤xn​)=i=1∏n​FXi​​(xi​),E[i=1∏n​hi​(Xi​)]=i=1∏n​E[hi​(Xi​)].​(16.1)
Independence holds exactly when the joint pmf, or the joint density when there is one, is the product of the marginals. The proof below covers pmfs; for densities the equivalence is stated without proof (Grinstead and Snell 1997, §4.2, Definition 4.7 and Theorem 4.2).

Proof of the equivalence for pmfs. Summing the product of the pmfs over the values up to each xi​ gives the first line of (16.1). Conversely, write the first line with x<x1​ in place of x1​, and let x rise to x1​. By continuity (LM13), the limit is the same equation with X1​<x1​ in place of X1​≤x1​ on both sides. Subtracting it from the first line leaves X1​=x1​ on both sides. Repeating the step for x2​,…,xn​ gives (13.13). ■

Proof of the product rule for two discrete variables. The joint pmf factorizes, so the double sum splits:

​E[h1​(X1​)h2​(X2​)]=x1​∑​h1​(x1​)pX1​​(x1​)x2​∑​h2​(x2​)pX2​​(x2​)=E[h1​(X1​)]E[h2​(X2​)].​

The finite expectations allow the sums in any order. A joint density splits the same way, as in LM5's Gaussian integral, and n variables repeat the step. ■

DefinitionCovariance and correlation

Let X and Y have finite variances. Their covariance is

Cov(X,Y)​:=E[(X−μX​)(Y−μY​)]=E[XY]−μX​μY​,​(16.2)
written σXY​. If also σX​,σY​>0, their correlation is ρXY​:=σXY​/(σX​σY​). It satisfies ∣ρXY​∣≤1, with equality exactly when Pr(Y=ηX+ζ)=1 for constants η=0 and ζ.

The second form follows from linearity (14.3). The bound copies LM8's proof of (8.6), with an expectation in place of the sum over dates (Deep Dive below).

Deep DiveWhy ∣ρXY​∣≤1, and when it equals 1optional · click to expand

Here δ>0 and W is a random variable. For every real η,

0​≤E[(Y−μY​−η(X−μX​))2]=σY2​−2ησXY​+η2σX2​.​
The choice η=σXY​/σX2​, LM8's closest multiple, gives 0≤σY2​−σXY2​/σX2​, so ∣ρXY​∣≤1.

Equality holds exactly when this expectation is 0. A variable W≥0 with EW=0 is 0 with probability one: Markov's inequality (14.7) gives Pr(W≥δ)≤EW/δ=0, and these events increase to {W>0} as δ falls (LM13). So Y=ηX+ζ with probability one, where ζ=μY​−ημX​ and η=0 since σY​>0. Conversely, Y=ηX+ζ gives ρXY​=ησX2​/(σX​∣η∣σX​)=±1.

Independence implies zero covariance: (16.1) with h1​ and h2​ the identity gives E[XY]=μX​μY​. Variables with zero covariance are uncorrelated. The converse fails.

Example 3Uncorrelated but dependent

Let X take the values −1, 0 and 1 with probability 1/3 each, and let Y=X2. Show that Cov(X,Y)=0 although Y is a function of X.

Solution

By (16.2), Cov(X,Y)=E[X3]−EXE[X2]=0−0×32​=0, since X3=X has mean 0. Yet Pr(Y=0∣X=0)=1 while Pr(Y=0)=31​, so the joint pmf is not the product of the marginals. Covariance measures only the linear part of a dependence, and this symmetric dependence has none.

Market data show the same pattern. Let Rt​ be the TAIEX price index's return (no dividends) on day t of the U28 dates.

Example 4Today's move and tomorrow's

For the 4,381 pairs (Rt​,Rt+1​), compute ρ^​(Rt​,Rt+1​) and ρ^​(∣Rt​∣,∣Rt+1​∣), and the mean of ∣Rt+1​∣ after the days with ∣Rt​∣≥2% and after the others.

Solution

The returns correlate 0.040, close to 0, while their sizes correlate 0.183. After the 306 days with ∣Rt​∣≥2%, the next day's size averaged 1.28%, against 0.75% after the others and 0.79% overall (Exhibit 3).

Under independence, both population correlations would be zero and the two conditional means equal. Large moves cluster in time, of either sign; LM26 models how tomorrow's spread depends on today's move.

Under the empirical distribution an expectation is an average with divisor T, so (16.2) is LM7's average product and ρXY​ is LM8's (8.9). The sample's 0.5749 is exactly the empirical model's correlation; as an estimate of another model's correlation, its error is LM20's subject. Orthogonal centred return vectors (LM8) are uncorrelated under this model, not independent.

PitfallA correlation near zero does not prevent a joint loss

In 2022 0050 and 00679B both fell about 21–22% while their daily correlation was −0.06 (LM7). Correlation concerns deviations from each asset's own mean; when both means turn negative, both assets lose, whatever the correlation.

導讀不相關不等於獨立

兩個隨機變數（random variable）獨立（independent），是指聯合分布（joint distribution）等於邊際分布（marginal distribution）的乘積；這時乘積的期望值（expectation）等於期望值的乘積，所以共變異數（covariance）為 0。反過來不成立：X 取 −1、0、1，Y=X2，兩者互不相關（uncorrelated），Y 卻完全由 X 決定。相關係數（correlation coefficient）只量線性的部分。加權股價指數今天與明天報酬的相關係數只有 0.040，報酬大小的相關係數卻是 0.183：大波動之後常跟著大波動，方向卻難說。樣本相關係數就是經驗分布（empirical distribution）這個母體（population）的相關係數，不是另一套定義。

Knowledge Check 2

For constants η=0 and ζ, how do Cov(X,ηY+ζ) and the correlation of X with ηY+ζ compare with Cov(X,Y) and ρXY​?

Answer

By (16.2), Cov(X,ηY+ζ)=E[(X−μX​)η(Y−μY​)]=ηCov(X,Y), since ζ cancels with the mean. The standard deviation becomes ∣η∣σY​ (14.4), so the correlation is ρXY​ for η>0 and −ρXY​ for η<0.

4Sums, Portfolios and Covariance Matrices

compute the mean and variance of sums and portfolios, and explain why every covariance matrix is positive semidefinite

LM7 expanded the variance of a two-asset portfolio's sample returns. The same expansion works for random variables.

TheoremVariance of a sum

Let X1​,…,Xn​ have EXi2​<∞ and covariances σij​:=Cov(Xi​,Xj​), so that σii​=VarXi​, and let a1​,…,an​ be constants. Then

Var(i∑​ai​Xi​)=i∑​j∑​ai​aj​σij​.(16.3)
If the Xi​ are uncorrelated, in particular if they are independent, then Var(∑i​Xi​)=∑i​VarXi​.

Proof. By linearity (14.3), the sum deviates from its mean by ∑i​ai​(Xi​−μXi​​). Square it, and take expectations term by term. For uncorrelated variables only the terms with i=j remain. ■

With two assets, (16.3) gives LM7's identities in population form: the portfolio variance σp2​=w12​σ12​+2w1​w2​σ12​+w22​σ22​ and Var(R1​−R2​)=σ12​+σ22​−2σ12​. Then (16.2) and linearity (14.3) give Cov(R1​,Rp​)=w1​σ12​+w2​σ12​. The theorem's last sentence, Var(∑i​Xi​)=∑i​VarXi​, needs only zero covariances, not independence, as LM3's sum of squared increments did.

Example 5A two-asset model

Take a model whose annualized covariance matrix for Semiconductor and FinancialInsurance is LM10's: σ12​=570.34, σ12​=261.83 and σ22​=363.73, in %². Find the variance and volatility of the 50/50 portfolio, Cov(R1​,Rp​) and the volatility of R1​−R2​.

Solution

By (16.3),

σp2​​=0.25(570.34)+2(0.25)(261.83)+0.25(363.73)=364.43,​
so σp​=19.09%. Next, by (16.2) and linearity, Cov(R1​,Rp​)=0.5(570.34)+0.5(261.83)=416.085, exactly. Finally, Var(R1​−R2​)=570.34+363.73−2(261.83)=410.41, a volatility of 20.26%, as LM10 found for (1,−1,0)⊤. Under the empirical distribution each value is also the sample value.

Sums over days use log returns, which add (LM1, (1.12)). Model the m daily log returns of a year as uncorrelated, each with mean g and standard deviation σr​. Their sum has mean mg by (14.3) and variance mσr2​ by (16.3): the assumption behind LM5's annualization.

For the TAIEX price index on U28 dates, take g=rˉ=0.05454% and σr​=sr​=1.1392% (divisor T), and m=245, the rounded A. The model year's log return has mean 245 × 0.05454% = 13.36% and standard deviation √245 × 1.1392% = 17.83% (a model fitted to the same days). If the days are iid, not only uncorrelated, a sum of many of them is nearly normal: the central limit theorem of LM17.

The same rule counts events. An indicator 1A​ with Pr(A)=p has mean p by (14.1) and, being its own square, variance p−p2 by (14.4). A count of n independent such indicators has mean np and variance np(1−p): LM15's binomial moments (15.2) in one line.

DefinitionMean vector and covariance matrix

Let X=(X1​,…,XN​)⊤ be a random vector with E∥X∥2<∞ and mean μ:=EX. Its covariance matrix Σ has entries σij​=Cov(Xi​,Xj​). For a J×N matrix M and vectors b and a of lengths J and N,

Σ:=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)⊤],Cov(MX+b)=MΣM⊤,a⊤Σa=Var(a⊤X)≥0,​(16.4)
where Cov of a vector means its covariance matrix. So Σ is positive semidefinite.

Proof. The vector MX+b deviates from its mean Mμ+b by M(X−μ). By linearity, entry by entry, its covariance matrix is E[M(X−μ)(X−μ)⊤M⊤]=MΣM⊤. With M=a⊤, a single row, this is a variance, never negative. ■

The correlation matrix Corr(X) is the covariance matrix of the entries Xi​/σi​, so it is positive semidefinite too. A portfolio return Rp​=w⊤R has variance σp2​=w⊤Σw. Under the empirical distribution, (16.4) gives LM10's (10.2), (10.3) and (10.5). Splitting σp2​ among assets is the work of LM27 and LM31; how far Σ^ lies from Σ is LM30's.

PitfallStandard deviations do not add

Only variances and covariances combine by (16.3). The 20.26% of Example 5 is neither 23.88 − 19.07 = 4.81 points nor √(570.34 + 363.73) = 30.56%. The first holds only when ρ=1, the second only when ρ=0.

Knowledge Check 3

Let X and Y be independent with variances 4 and 9. Find Var(X−Y) and the correlation of X with X+Y.

Answer

Independent variables are uncorrelated, so (16.3) gives Var(X−Y)=4+9=13: a difference adds variances too. Next, Cov(X,X+Y)=VarX=4 and Var(X+Y)=13, so the correlation is 4/(213​)=0.555.

5Conditional Expectation

apply conditional expectation, the tower property and the law of total variance

The conditional density of Example 2 changes with x, so the mean of Y given X=x changes too.

DefinitionConditional expectation

Let E∣Y∣<∞. For pX​(x)>0, the conditional expectation of Y given X=x is h(x)=E[Y∣X=x]:=∑y​ypY∣X​(y∣x); with densities, it is ∫yfY∣X​(y∣x)dy. The random variable E[Y∣X]:=h(X) is the conditional expectation of Y given X. The conditional variance Var(Y∣X=x) is E[(Y−h(x))2∣X=x], and Var(Y∣X) is that function evaluated at X.

For Example 2,

E[Y∣X=x]​=∫01​yx+21​x+y​dy=x+1/2x/2+1/3​=6x+33x+2​.​

The conditional mean falls from 2/3 at x=0 to 5/9 at x=1.

On an event {X∈S} with Pr(X∈S)>0, the conditional mean is the average over the event:

E[X∣X∈S]=Pr(X∈S)E[X1{X∈S}]​.

LM5's tail mean (5.11) is this formula for a normal X and the values below a threshold.

TheoremTower property and law of total variance

If E∣Y∣<∞, then

E[E[Y∣X]]=EY.(16.5)
If EY2<∞, then
VarY​=E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var(E[Y∣X]).​(16.6)

Proof for discrete variables. The events {X=x} partition the sample space, and total probability (13.8) gives pY​(y)=∑x​pX​(x)pY∣X​(y∣x). Hence

EY​=y∑​yx∑​pX​(x)pY∣X​(y∣x)=x∑​pX​(x)h(x),​

which is (16.5); the finite E∣Y∣ allows the exchange of sums. For (16.6), square Y−μY​=(Y−h(X))+(h(X)−μY​). Given X=x, the cross term has conditional mean (h(x)−μY​)(h(x)−h(x))=0. Taking expectations with (16.5) leaves E[Var(Y∣X)] and Var(h(X)). With densities, sums become integrals. ■

So (16.6) splits a variance into the average variance within the groups {X=x} and the variance of the group means between them. On the empirical distribution both parts are exact sums over days.

Example 6FinancialInsurance's variance, split by Semiconductor's bin

Let X be Semiconductor's bin of Exhibit 2 and Y FinancialInsurance's return in %, on a day drawn from U28's empirical distribution. Use Exhibit 4 to check (16.5) and (16.6), and find the share of VarY that the bin explains.

Solution

The weights are 859, 2,519 and 1,004 days over 4,382. The tower property gives FinancialInsurance's mean:

​[859(−0.9505)+2,519(0.0730)+1,004(0.8458)]/4,382=0.0494%.​
With the same weights, the squared standard deviations average 1.140 (%²), the within part. The weighted variance of the three means about 0.0494 is 0.342, the between part. Their sum, 1.482, is FinancialInsurance's variance, and the bin explains 0.342/1.482=23.1% of it.

A normal model would explain ρ^​2=0.3305 with its linear conditional mean (Section 6), using Semiconductor's return itself.

PitfallGroup means are weighted by the groups' probabilities

The plain average of the three means in Exhibit 4 is −0.0106%, the wrong sign for a sector whose mean is 0.0494%. The tower property weights each mean by pX​(x), and the middle bin holds 57% of the days.

導讀條件期望值與全變異數法則

條件期望值（conditional expectation）E[Y∣X] 是「知道 X 之後對 Y 的平均」，它是 X 的函數，所以本身也是隨機變數（random variable）。雙重期望值定理（tower property）說，把各組的條件平均按各組的機率加權平均，就回到 EY。權重一定要用機率，等權平均會得到錯的答案。全變異數法則（law of total variance）把變異數（variance）拆成「組內變異數的平均」加上「組平均數（mean）之間的變異數」。以半導體的報酬分三組時，金融保險的變異數 1.482 中有 23.1% 落在組間；在經驗分布（empirical distribution）上，這兩條公式都是精確的恆等式。

Knowledge Check 4

LM5 found E[Z∣Z≤−2]=−2.3732 for a standard normal Z (its Problem 14). Write it as a conditional expectation on an event.

Answer

With S=(−∞,−2], it is E[Z1{Z≤−2}]/Pr(Z≤−2). The numerator is ∫−∞−2​zφ(z)dz=−φ(2), the denominator Φ(−2)=0.02275, and the ratio −2.3732: an average over the tail.

6The Multivariate Normal Distribution

describe the multivariate normal through linear maps, colouring, marginals and conditional distributions
define the chi-square law, and interpret probability contours and the squared Mahalanobis distance against it

LM12 coloured standard normal draws with a Cholesky factor to simulate returns. This section defines the law of such draws.

DefinitionMultivariate normal

A random vector X of length N is multivariate normal when every combination a⊤X is normal, a constant counting as normal with variance 0. Its law is written NN​(μ,Σ), with μ and Σ as in (16.4).

Two facts are stated without proof: independent normal variables are jointly normal, and μ and Σ fix a normal vector's law. Durrett (2019, §3.10 and Exercise 3.10.8) gives both for every positive semidefinite Σ, through characteristic functions.

TheoremLinear maps, colouring and the density

Let X∼NN​(μ,Σ) with Σ=LL⊤, and let M be a J×N matrix and b a vector of length J. Then

MX+b∼NJ​(Mμ+b,MΣM⊤),μ+LZ∼NN​(μ,Σ)  for  Z∼NN​(0,I).​(16.7)
If Σ is positive definite, X has the density
fX​(x)=(2π)−N/2(detΣ)−1/2e−d2/2,d2:=(x−μ)⊤Σ−1(x−μ),​
where d2 is the squared Mahalanobis distance (stated without proof; Wasserman 2004, §2.10, equation (2.10) and Theorem 2.43).

Proof of the two lines. For any a, the variable a⊤(MX+b)=(M⊤a)⊤X+a⊤b is normal, so MX+b is multivariate normal, with the moments of (16.4). Independent standard normals form Z∼NN​(0,I) by the first stated fact; take M=L and b=μ. ■

The second line is colouring in population form, and L−1(X−μ)∼NN​(0,I) is whitening. LM12's whitened returns are only uncorrelated with variance 1, in the sample; the model's Z has independent normal entries. Drawing Z on a computer is LM18's subject.

With M a row of the identity, (16.7) makes each Xi​ normal; with several rows, any sub-vector is multivariate normal. For an orthogonal matrix such as LM11's Q, (16.7) gives QZ∼NN​(0,I): a standard normal vector looks the same in every rotated frame.

If Σ is diagonal with every σi​>0, d2=∑i​(xi​−μi​)2/σi2​ and the density factorizes, so uncorrelated entries of a normal vector are independent. An entry of variance 0 is constant with probability one (Section 3's Deep Dive), so it is independent of the others too.

Deep DiveThe density for N=2optional · click to expand

Here X=μ+LZ by colouring, and x=μ+Lz is the image of a point z of the plane. The vector Z has the density φ(z1​)φ(z2​)=e−∥z∥2/2/(2π). The map sends a small square at z to a parallelogram spanned by L's columns, so areas grow by ∣detL∣=l11​l22​ (LM9, (9.2)). Both small regions have the same probability, so

fX​(x)l11​l22​=2πe−∥z∥2/2​.
Since detΣ=(l11​l22​)2 and ∥z∥2=d2 by (12.9), this is (16.7)'s density for N=2.

TheoremThe conditional law in a normal pair

Let (X,Y) be a normal pair with σX​,σY​>0 and correlation ρ, and let β:=σXY​/σX2​. Then

Y=μY​+β(X−μX​)+ε,ε∼N(0,σY2​(1−ρ2)),​(16.8)
with ε independent of X. Given X=x, Y is normal with mean μY​+β(x−μX​) and variance σY2​(1−ρ2).

Proof. Define ε by (16.8). The pair (X,ε) is a linear map of (X,Y) plus a constant, so it is jointly normal, as in the proof of (16.7). Since Cov(X,ε)=σXY​−βσX2​=0, X and ε are independent. By (16.3),

Varε​=σY2​−2βσXY​+β2σX2​=σY2​−σX2​σXY2​​=σY2​(1−ρ2).​

Fixing X=x leaves the law of the independent ε unchanged. ■

The slope β is the population slope that LM12's least squares estimate; its standard error is LM23's. Since Var(E[Y∣X])=β2σX2​=ρ2σY2​, the share between in (16.6) is ρ2.

Example 7Semiconductor falls 5%

Model the pair as normal with the sample's daily moments (divisor T): means 0.0947% and 0.0494%, standard deviations 1.5243% and 1.2173%, ρ=0.5749. Given a Semiconductor return of −5%, find FinancialInsurance's conditional mean, standard deviation and probability of a fall of 3% or more, and compare the data.

Solution

The slope is β=0.5749×1.2173/1.5243=0.4591. By (16.8), the conditional mean, the standard deviation (LM12's l22​) and the probability are

​E[Y∣X=−5%]=0.0494+0.4591×(−5−0.0947)=−2.29%,1.21731−0.57492​=0.996%,Pr(Y≤−3%∣X=−5%)=Φ((−3+2.29)/0.996)=Φ(−0.713)=0.238.​
Unrounded inputs agree.

On the 17 days with Semiconductor between −5.5% and −4.5%, FinancialInsurance averaged −2.86%, with a standard deviation of 2.00% (divisor 17). Six fell 3% or more: lower and wider than the model, on few days.

DefinitionChi-square law

Let Z1​,…,ZN​ be independent standard normal variables. The law of Z12​+⋯+ZN2​ is the chi-square distribution with N degrees of freedom, χN2​. Its mean is N, since EZi2​=1 (LM5). Its variance is 2N, since Var(Zi2​)=2 by (14.6) and the squares are uncorrelated by (16.1), so (16.3) applies.

TheoremMahalanobis distance of a normal vector

If X∼NN​(μ,Σ) with Σ positive definite, the squared Mahalanobis distance of X has the law χN2​. For N=2,

Pr(d2>k2)=e−k2/2.(16.9)

Proof. Whitening gives Z=L−1(X−μ)∼NN​(0,I), and d2=∥Z∥2 because Σ−1=L−⊤L−1, as in (12.9). For N=2, LM5's disc integral gives Pr(Z12​+Z22​≤k2)=1−e−k2/2. ■

For N>2, SciPy's stats.chi2 gives the tails of χN2​, and LM21 builds tests on it.

The density (16.7) is constant where d2 is. With Σ's eigenpairs, (11.3) gives Σ−1=∑i​qi​qi⊤​/λi​, so the contour d2=k2 is an ellipse (for N>2, an ellipsoid) with semi-axes kλi​​ along the eigenvectors qi​ of (11.1). It holds the probability Pr(χN2​≤k2). For the pair, Σ^ has entries 2.323354, 1.066603 and 1.481729 in %² (LM12), and (11.2) gives λ1​=3.049 and λ2​=0.756. LM11's ellipse on LM7's sample was a description; under a normal model it becomes a probability contour (Exhibit 5).

Example 8Days outside the circle of radius 3

Under the normal model for the pair, find the probability that a day lies outside the whitened circle of radius 3. Among n=4,382 independent days, find the mean and standard deviation of the count of such days.

Solution

By (16.9), p=Pr(d2>9)=e−4.5=0.011109, about 1.11%. The count of n independent indicators is Bin(n,p) ((15.1), (15.2)), with mean np=48.68, variance np(1−p)=48.14 and standard deviation 6.94.

The data hold 177 such days (Exhibit 6), set beside the model's mean and spread, not divided by them. Whether such a gap could be chance is LM21's question, and the model's Σ comes from the same days.

Example 9How rare is 7 April 2025 under a normal model?

LM12 found d2=89.30 for S5 on 7 April 2025, the largest of the 4,382 days. Under a normal model with S5's sample moments, how likely is a day at least that far out?

Solution

By (16.9), d2∼χ52​, and stats.chi2.sf(89.30, 5) gives 9.4×10−18: at A=245.48, once in about 4×1014 years. 184 days lie beyond the 99.9% quantile 20.52, where the model expects 4.4 (Exhibit 6). The 10% limit capped the day (LM12), so even 89.30 understates the shock.

Exhibit 7 lists the population counterparts of earlier sample results.

PitfallNormal marginals do not make a normal vector

A pair can have two standard normal marginals and zero covariance and still be dependent. The rule "uncorrelated implies independent" needs the pair to be jointly normal, not only each marginal.

導讀多變量常態分布與 Mahalanobis 距離

多變量常態分布（multivariate normal distribution）的定義是：任何線性組合（linear combination）都是常態分布（normal distribution）。把獨立（independent）的標準常態（standard normal）變數乘上 Cholesky 因子 L 再加上 μ，就得到共變異數矩陣（covariance matrix）為 Σ 的常態向量，這是著色（colouring）；反過來乘上 L−1 就是白化（whitening）。LM12 的樣本白化後只保證互不相關（uncorrelated）且變異數（variance）為 1，模型裡的 Z 卻是獨立的常態，兩者差很多。常態向量的 Mahalanobis 距離（Mahalanobis distance）平方服從自由度（degrees of freedom）為 N 的卡方分布（chi-square distribution），二維時落在半徑 k 之外的機率是 e−k2/2。半導體與金融保險這一對，模型預期約 49 天落在半徑 3 之外，實際有 177 天；這個差距是否可能出於偶然，留待 LM21。

Knowledge Check 5

For S5, 7 April 2025 has the sample's largest dt2​. Among U28's 28 sectors its dt2​ is 132.29 and ranks only 15th; the largest, 209.55, falls on 5 May 2009. Why?

Answer

Deviations along directions of little variance count far more. On 7 April 2025, 97.1% of the squared deviation lies along the first eigenvector of Σ^, LM11's common move, whose variance is large. On 5 May 2009 the sectors ran from −3.71% to +6.06% while the TAIEX price index rose 0.78%, a dispersion that the small eigenvalues rarely allow.

7Correlation in a Crash

compare a crash correlation with the bivariate normal benchmark under the same conditioning event

The case's three days gave a correlation of 0.851, against 0.5749 for the whole sample. All 28 sectors fell together on 156 days (LM11). A higher correlation on bad days looks like contagion. Yet a normal pair with one fixed ρ also shows another correlation on selected days.

TheoremCorrelation given an event of one variable

Let (X,Y) be a normal pair with σX​,σY​>0 and correlation ρ. Let {X∈S} be an event with Pr(X∈S)>0 on which X has a positive conditional variance σS2​. Then

​Corr(X,Y∣X∈S)=ρ2+(1−ρ2)σX2​/σS2​​ρ​.​(16.10)
(Boyer, Gibson and Loretan 1999, Theorem 1.)

Proof. By (16.8), Y=μY​+β(X−μX​)+ε with ε independent of X, hence of the event, on which it keeps its mean 0 and variance σY2​(1−ρ2). Conditionally, Cov(X,Y)=βσS2​ and VarY=β2σS2​+σY2​(1−ρ2) by (16.3). Divide by the two standard deviations, put β=ρσY​/σX​, and cancel σY​σS​/σX​. ■

The correlation rises when the event widens the spread of X and falls when it narrows it. Moves of k standard deviations either way widen it; a one-sided tail, whose values lie close together, narrows it. Forbes and Rigobon (2002) adjust crisis correlations this way before reading them as contagion.

Deep DiveConditional variances of a standard normaloptional · click to expand

Here ℓ:=φ(k)/Φ(−k) for k≥0. Integration by parts, as LM5 found EZ2=1, gives

∫−∞−k​z2φ(z)dz​=[−zφ(z)]−∞−k​+∫−∞−k​φ(z)dz=kφ(k)+Φ(−k).​
Dividing by Φ(−k) gives E[Z2∣Z≤−k]=1+kℓ, and (5.11) gives E[Z∣Z≤−k]=−ℓ. Hence
Var(Z∣Z≤−k)=1+kℓ−ℓ2,Var(Z∣∣Z∣≥k)=1+kℓ,​
the second because the two-sided event has mean 0 and equal tails. At k=2, ℓ=2.3732 (LM5, Problem 14), and the variances are 0.1143 and 5.7464, which enter (16.10) with σX2​=1.

Exhibit 8 applies (16.10) to the pair with ρ=0.5749 and sets the data beside it.

Those events condition on one variable. An exceedance correlation conditions on both: both returns lie k standard deviations or more below their means, or both above (Longin and Solnik 2001; Ang and Chen 2002). For a normal pair and k>0 it has no closed form in φ and Φ; the script integrates it with quad, as LM5 did (Exhibit 9).

Example 10Did the correlation rise in the crash?

Express Semiconductor's moves on 7–9 April 2025 in standard deviations, from LM10's returns and Example 7's moments. Then compare the pair's conditional correlations with the normal benchmark under the same events.

Solution

The moves are (−9.95−0.0947)/1.5243=−6.59, −2.68 and −2.99 standard deviations (unrounded inputs give −3.00 for 9 April). Three days cannot measure a correlation, and the first, the sample's extreme, was capped by the 10% limit. Use Exhibit 8 and Exhibit 9 instead.

When Semiconductor moved 2 standard deviations either way (223 days), the data give 0.788 against the model's 0.860; at 1, 0.692 against 0.745. Larger moves alone account for these correlations above 0.5749.

One-sided events differ. Semiconductor's falls of 2 give 0.488 against 0.231 (105 days). Joint falls of 2 give 0.669 against 0.156 (44 days), and joint rises 0.541 against 0.156 (32 days). Falls exceed the model more than rises, as Longin and Solnik (2001) report, but on few days.

The widget sets the event, ρ and k. Its model values for joint events are interpolated in ρ from a grid, with errors below 10−5 in the correlation and 0.01 days in the count. It opens on joint falls of 2 at ρ=0.5749: the model gives 0.156 with probability 0.0051 (22.4 days), the pair 0.669 on 44 days.

Models that keep each marginal and change only the dependence, notably in the tails, are called copulas; this book does not use them.

PitfallCompare a conditional correlation with the model's, not with the full sample's

The two-sided 0.788 exceeds the full-sample 0.5749, yet a normal pair with the constant correlation 0.5749 gives 0.860 for the same event. Compare a conditional correlation with the model under the same event; whether a gap could be chance is for LM21 and LM22.

導讀崩盤時的相關係數：和同一事件下的模型比

只挑大波動的日子算相關係數（correlation coefficient），常態模型本身就會給出不同的數字：條件相關係數（conditional correlation）取決於條件事件（conditioning event）下 X 的變異數（variance）。雙邊的大波動讓 X 的變異數變大，相關係數跟著上升；單邊的尾部讓變異數變小，相關係數反而下降。所以崩盤時的相關係數要和「同一事件下的常態模型」比，不能和全樣本的 0.5749 比。半導體大漲或大跌 2 個標準差（standard deviation）時，資料是 0.788，模型是 0.860；兩者同時下跌 2 個標準差時，資料是 0.669，模型只有 0.156。在 2 個標準差時，超越相關係數（exceedance correlation）的下跌端（0.669）高於上漲端（0.541），方向與 Longin 和 Solnik（2001）一致，但這些天數很少。

Knowledge Check 6

In a normal pair with ρ=0.5749, what is the correlation on the days when ∣X−μX​∣≥σX​, given Var(Z∣∣Z∣≥1)=2.5251?

Answer

By (16.10),

​0.57492+(1−0.57492)/2.5251​0.5749​=0.745.​
The data give 0.692 on 1,088 days (Exhibit 8).

8Joint Distributions in Python

compute joint frequencies, conditional moments, Mahalanobis distances and normal benchmarks in Python with the right divisor, guard and tail function

Counts at an edge use a guard, because index levels have two decimals and a return can equal −1% exactly (LM5). np.cov divides by T−1 unless ddof=0 (or bias=True) is passed, while (10.2) divides by T. Mahalanobis distances come from a Cholesky factor and a triangular solve, never from an inverse.

Python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from scipy.linalg import solve_triangular

# x1, x2: the pair's T daily returns (Semiconductor, FinancialInsurance)
EPS = 1e-12                               # guard for edges such as -1%
both = (x1 <= -0.01 + EPS) & (x2 <= -0.01 + EPS)
print(both.sum())                         # 347 days, the corner cell
XP = np.column_stack([x1, x2])
S = np.cov(XP, rowvar=False, ddof=0)      # divisor T, as (10.2)
L = np.linalg.cholesky(S)                 # lower factor, S = L L'
Z = solve_triangular(L, (XP - XP.mean(axis=0)).T, lower=True)
d2 = (Z**2).sum(axis=0)                   # d_t^2 of every day
print((d2 > 9 + EPS).sum())               # 177
print(len(d2) * stats.chi2.sf(9, 2))      # 48.68 expected
print(1 - stats.chi2.cdf(89.30, 5))       # 0.0: the tail is lost
print(stats.chi2.sf(89.30, 5))            # 9.4e-18
PitfallA tail probability from 1 - cdf can vanish

stats.chi2.cdf(89.30, 5) differs from 1 by less than 10−17. Double precision has no number between 1−1.1×10−16 and 1, so the result is stored as 1 and 1 - cdf returns 0.0. stats.chi2.sf computes the upper tail directly: 9.4×10−18.

In PythonCompanion lab

The Polars-first notebook LM16_lab.ipynb repairs the sector closes, rebuilds the module's exhibits and computational examples, and solves the computational practice problems. It ends with a stability check that compares the two price-limit regimes.

The notebook reads FinMind files that you download once with your own token. From the repository root, run uv run python data/fetch_finmind.py, then uv run python data/make_lab_data.py. FinMind's licence does not allow the book to redistribute the data. After that, the notebook runs offline.

Knowledge Check 7

Why does np.corrcoef need no ddof argument?

Answer

The divisor appears once in the covariance and once, through the two square roots, in the product of standard deviations, so it cancels, as in (8.9).

Summary

  • A conditional law divides a slice of the joint law by its marginal: FinancialInsurance fell 1% or more on 0.404 of Semiconductor's falls, against 0.1228 of all days.
  • Independence makes covariance zero, (16.1), but not conversely: the TAIEX price index's returns correlate 0.040 day to day, their sizes 0.183.
  • Covariance and correlation (16.2) are the population versions of LM7's and LM8's statistics.
  • Variances of sums follow (16.3); covariance matrices are positive semidefinite, (16.4).
  • By (16.5) and (16.6), Semiconductor's bin explains 23.1% of FinancialInsurance's variance.
  • By (16.9), a normal model expects 48.68 days outside radius 3 for the pair (standard deviation 6.94); the data hold 177.
  • Conditioning changes a normal pair's correlation, (16.10): 0.860 for moves of 2 either way and 0.156 for joint falls of 2, against the pair's 0.788 and 0.669.

Explain why 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(89.30, 5) and stats.chi2.sf(89.30, 5) differ.

Solutions

  1. B is correct: 347/859=0.404. A is the joint probability 347/4,382=0.079. C conditions the wrong way, 347/538=0.645.

  2. A is correct. Here EX=∫01​x(x+21​)dx=127​ and E[XY]=∫01​∫01​xy(x+y)dydx=31​, so Cov(X,Y)=31​−14449​=−1441​=−0.0069. With VarX=14411​ the correlation is −111​=−0.0909. B omits μX​μY​; C assumes independence, which Example 2 excluded.

  3. C is correct. By symmetry, Pr(Y≤y)=21​Φ(y)+21​Pr(−X≤y)=Φ(y). By (16.1), Cov(X,Y)=E[S]E[X2]=0, yet ∣Y∣=∣X∣. A needs joint normality. B fails: X+Y=0 with probability 1/2, while for a normal pair with ρ=0, X+Y∼N(0,2) gives each single value probability 0.

  4. By (16.3), Var(R1​−R2​)=0.04+0.0225−2(0.5)(0.20)(0.15)=0.0325, a volatility of 18.03%. Next, Cov(R1​,Rp​)=0.6(0.04)+0.4(0.015)=0.0300, and σp2​=0.36(0.04)+2(0.24)(0.015)+0.16(0.0225)=0.0252, so σp​=15.87%. The correlation is 0.0300/(0.20×0.1587)=0.945. The value 5% is ∣σ1​−σ2​∣, right only for ρ=1; 25% is σ12​+σ22​​, right only for ρ=0.

  5. By (16.3), the variance is msr2​ plus twice the m−1 adjacent covariances 0.04sr2​. The factor is 1+2(0.04)(244/245)=1.0797, and the standard deviation is 17.83%×1.0797​=18.53%. Wrong routes: 245 × 1.1392% = 279.1% adds standard deviations, and 17.83% × 1.0797 = 19.25% applies a variance factor to a standard deviation. This is a model; LM19 examines the data.

  6. By (16.5), (306×0.2251+4,075×0.0496)/4,381=0.0619%. By (16.6), within 1.288 plus between 0.002 gives the total 1.290 (%²), a share between of 0.2% (0.155%). The between part is tiny (0.002 of 1.290), but the spreads differ by a factor of 1.8889/1.0570 = 1.79, which a correlation of returns cannot see. The equal-weight mean, (0.2251 + 0.0496)/2 = 0.13735%, ignores that big days are rare.

  7. By (16.8), the mean is 0.0494+0.4591×(−3−0.0947)=−1.37%, and the standard deviation stays 0.996%. Then (−2+1.37)/0.996=−0.6325 and Φ(−0.6325)=0.264. The unconditional standard deviation would give Φ(−0.63/1.2173)=0.302, and the slope ρ in place of β a mean of −1.73%.

  8. Forward substitution gives

    z1​z2​​=(−9.48−0.0947)/1.5243=−6.281,=(−6.93−0.0494−0.6998z1​)/0.9960=−2.594,​
    so d2=46.18; unrounded inputs give 46.22. By (16.9), Pr(d2>46.18)=e−23.09=9.4×10−11, about 4×10−7 expected days in 4,382.

  9. (a) By (16.3), Var(X/σX​±Y/σY​)=2±2ρXY​≥0, so −1≤ρXY​≤1. If ρXY​=1, then X/σX​−Y/σY​ has variance 0, so it is constant with probability one (Section 3's Deep Dive): Y=μY​+(σY​/σX​)(X−μX​). (b) The deviation M(X−μ) gives MΣM⊤ by linearity. With M=diag(σi​)−1 this is Corr(X), positive semidefinite by (16.4).

  10. By (16.10),

    ​0.57492+(1−0.57492)/5.7464​0.5749​=0.860,​
    and with 0.1143 the result is 0.231. The two-sided event widens the spread of X (variance 5.7464 against 1) and raises the correlation; the one-sided tail narrows it (0.1143) and lowers it. The data's 0.788 lies below 0.860, while their 0.488 lies far above 0.231.

  11. B is correct, the benchmark of Exhibit 9 at k=2. A ignores the conditioning. C is the benchmark for moves of one variable either way (Problem 10).

  12. Both methods give Exhibit 2, since no return is exactly ±1%. The pair has 177 days with dt2​>9 against the model's 48.68. The difference 1 - cdf returns 0.0 and sf returns 9.4e-18, as Section 8's pitfall explains.

Glossary

Term 中文 Meaning
Joint distribution 聯合分布 The law of several random variables together: a joint pmf, density or distribution function.
Marginal distribution 邊際分布 The law of one variable, obtained from the joint law by summing or integrating the others out.
Conditional distribution 條件分布 The law of Y given X=x: the joint pmf or density divided by the marginal of X.
Independent 獨立 Random variables whose joint distribution function factorizes, (16.1).
Covariance 共變異數 E[(X−μX​)(Y−μY​)], (16.2).
Correlation 相關係數 σXY​/(σX​σY​), between −1 and 1.
Uncorrelated 互不相關 With covariance zero; implied by independence, not conversely.
Covariance matrix 共變異數矩陣 Σ=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)⊤], positive semidefinite, (16.4).
Conditional expectation 條件期望值 E[Y∣X=x], the mean of the conditional law; E[Y∣X] is that function of X.
Tower property 雙重期望值定理 E[E[Y∣X]]=EY, (16.5).
Law of total variance 全變異數法則 Variance = mean within-group variance + variance of group means, (16.6).
Multivariate normal distribution 多變量常態分布 A random vector all of whose combinations are normal, NN​(μ,Σ), (16.7).
Colouring, whitening 著色、白化 μ+LZ and L−1(X−μ), with Σ=LL⊤.
Mahalanobis distance Mahalanobis 距離 d, with d2=(x−μ)⊤Σ−1(x−μ).
Chi-square distribution 卡方分布 The law χN2​ of a sum of N independent squared standard normals: mean N, variance 2N.
Degrees of freedom 自由度 The number N of squared standard normals in χN2​.
Conditional correlation 條件相關係數 The correlation given an event, (16.10) for a normal pair.
Exceedance correlation 超越相關係數 The correlation on the days when both variables lie beyond k standard deviations on the same side.
